script.opening: "Hello doctor — yes, I’ve been expecting your call. Before you start: I feel perfectly well. The only thing wrong with me is a watch my grandson set up that won’t stop tutting at me. If you’re ringing to tell me my heart’s skipping about a bit at my age — well, whose isn’t? I’ve buried a husband and kept a shop for forty years; a wobbly tick doesn’t frighten me."

facts.text: Genuinely none: no palpitations, breathlessness, chest pain, dizziness or blackouts. Walks the dog 40 minutes daily, gardens, drives to the garden centre. "Fit as a flea, bar the blood pressure."

If discussed: AF confirmed on 12-lead, rate 88, BP 138/82 on amlodipine. CHA₂DS₂-VASc: age 72 (65–74 scores 1), female (1), hypertension (1) = 3. ORBIT/bleeding: no anaemia, no renal disease, no falls history herself, no antiplatelets.

The buried layer, surfacing the moment anticoagulation is mentioned: Gordon was on warfarin for his valve. January 2021: slipped on ice outside the butcher’s, "a silly little fall, didn’t even break his glasses" — dead in three days from a bleed on the brain. "The blood thinner killed him, doctor. The fall was nothing. It was the warfarin. And now you want to put ME on it."
Polite refusal, pre-loaded: "I’ll take an aspirin if it makes you happy." Has already mentioned it to her neighbour ("Eileen says her cardiologist swears by aspirin").

That untreated AF’s strokes are typically LARGE and disabling; that aspirin gives little AF protection with real bleed risk (NICE NG196 advises against aspirin alone); that DOACs are not warfarin — no INR clinics, lower intracranial bleed rates, and her risk profile is favourable.

To be left alone with her dog and her garden. What she needs: the stroke maths made personal and honest, Gordon’s death respected AND distinguished, the aspirin myth retired, and a decision SHE owns — possibly not today.

ice.ideas: "A wobbly tick at my age" — normal wear, over-monitored by a fussy watch. Aspirin would be a reasonable compromise.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — Gordon. Warfarin, the ice, the bleed, three days. In her ledger the anticoagulant is the murder weapon, and the doctor on this phone is proposing it for her. She has already decided to refuse; the call is her being polite about it.
ice.expectations: To decline nicely and get back to the garden. Needs: unrushed honesty, the distinction between Gordon’s situation and hers made precisely, the aspirin escape-hatch closed kindly, and genuine permission to take time — a second call, the grandson involved if she wishes.

cues: "Whose isn’t, at my age?" — normalisation as armour; the watch is tutting at something real.
The temperature drops the instant "blood thinner" is said — Gordon arriving before his name does.
"I’ll take an aspirin if it makes you happy" — the compromise offer; accepting it fails her, refusing it bluntly loses her.

checkpoints.text: Explains AF in plain pictures (the top chambers quivering, blood eddying in a pouch, clots forming and travelling to the brain) and why FEELING well and BEING at risk coexist — the watch caught what symptoms never would

Does the stroke maths transparently and personally: CHA₂DS₂-VASc 3 (NICE NG196: offer anticoagulation at 2 or more) → about 3 in 100 per year untreated (Friberg, Eur Heart J 2012), compounding yearly; AF strokes are characteristically large and disabling; anticoagulation cuts the risk by about two-thirds (warfarin vs control: Hart, Ann Intern Med 2007; DOACs at least as effective: Ruff, Lancet 2014)

Retires the aspirin myth explicitly and kindly (NICE NG196: do not offer aspirin monotherapy solely for stroke prevention in AF): little protection against AF clots, with real bleeding risk — "the worst of both worlds"; Eileen’s cardiologist is either misquoted or out of date

Distinguishes DOACs from warfarin precisely: no INR clinics or food rules, shorter action, and — the sentence that matters — substantially LOWER rates of the exact bleed that killed Gordon; her own bleeding-risk screen (ORBIT, NICE NG196) is favourable and will be optimised (BP, falls review, no NSAIDs, alcohol) — and NG196 is clear that age or falls risk alone is not a reason to withhold anticoagulation
Hears the temperature drop and goes to it: "Tell me about Gordon" — the ice, the three days — received in full before any pharmacology is offered

Honours the ledger AND corrects it: Gordon’s warfarin was non-negotiable (metal valve), unmonitorable luck, and a different drug class; grieving the warfarin is fair — sentencing her own brain to unprotected AF in his memory is not what he’d sign

Hands the decision back with structure, not pressure: a thinking week, written information, the grandson welcome on the next call, the door explicitly open — refusal documented as today’s decision, never the final one

Safety-nets regardless of her decision: FAST symptoms = 999 said plainly; rate/symptom triggers (breathless, faint, fluttering) named; bloods (U&E with creatinine clearance, LFT, FBC, thyroid function) arranged to keep the DOAC option live; the second call BOOKED — and the watch, reframed: "let it keep tutting; it’s the best cardiology nurse you’ve ever had"

worked.txt: "Let me draw what the watch found. The top chambers of your heart have stopped beating and started quivering — like a washing machine stuck on shimmer. The blood in one little pouch up there stops moving briskly, and still blood clots. If a clot breaks loose, the next stop is the brain. That’s the whole story — and you can feel completely well through every chapter of it except the last one."

"Your particular numbers — age, blood pressure, being a woman — put you at roughly a three-in-a-hundred chance of a stroke THIS year — about one in thirty — and the dice get rolled again every year. And AF strokes aren’t the small kind — they’re the ones that take the speech or the side. The tablet cuts that risk by about two-thirds. That’s the trade on the table."

"Sylvia — when I said blood thinner, everything went quiet. Tell me about Gordon. … Three days. From a fall that didn’t break his glasses. I understand completely why, in your ledger, the warfarin is what killed him — and on the ice that day, it played its part. I’m not going to argue with your grief. I’m going to ask permission to show you what’s different — about the drug, and about you."

"Three differences, counted on fingers. One: Gordon had a metal valve — warfarin or nothing, no choice, no modern option allowed even today. Two: warfarin is the old drug — the new ones don’t need blood-test clinics, leave the body quickly, and crucially have markedly LOWER rates of the exact bleed that took him. Three: you’re not Gordon — no ice-skating valve, good kidneys, steady on your feet, and a doctor who’ll tune your blood pressure and ban ibuprofen before we start anything."

"And the aspirin olive branch — I’m handing it back, kindly. Against AF clots, aspirin is a paper umbrella: nearly no protection, and it still makes you bleed easier. It’s the worst of both worlds, which is why the guidelines retired it years ago. Eileen’s cardiologist either treats something different or got quoted over a fence."

"Here’s what I’d like, and notice it isn’t a prescription: take the week. I’ll post you the plain-English version of everything I’ve said. Bring your grandson onto the next call if you want a second pair of ears — he started all this with that watch, he can finish it. And whatever you decide, two things hold: any face-drooping, arm-weakness or jumbled words is 999 that minute — and that watch stays on. It’s the best cardiology nurse you’ve ever had."

f.learning: Incidental, asymptomatic AF is a stroke-prevention consultation in disguise: explain the quivering-pouch mechanism (well-feeling and high-risk coexist), personalise CHA₂DS₂-VASc into honest annual odds (score 3: about 3% a year, Friberg 2012; offer anticoagulation at 2 or more, NICE NG196), retire aspirin explicitly (NICE NG196: not for stroke prevention alone; little protection, real bleed risk), and distinguish DOACs from warfarin — no INR monitoring, lower intracranial-bleed rates (about half, Ruff, Lancet 2014). The hidden agenda is the warfarin ghost: a spouse’s fatal bleed makes the anticoagulant the villain of the family story. Hear the grief in full BEFORE the pharmacology, honour the ledger while correcting its categories (valve = forced warfarin; she = neither), and hand the decision back with structure — a thinking week, written information, a booked second call. Refusal is today’s decision, never the final one.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG196 (atrial fibrillation) · BNF (direct-acting oral anticoagulants) · DVLA Assessing fitness to drive
knowledge.summary: Asymptomatic AF found by a wearable and confirmed on ECG is a stroke-prevention decision. Her CHA₂DS₂-VASc is 3, so anticoagulation with a DOAC should be offered; aspirin is not an alternative.

points.t: A wearable alert needs ECG confirmation, which she has. Rate 88 at rest with no symptoms means rate control is not the pressing issue; stroke risk is. Baseline FBC, U&E with creatinine clearance, LFTs and thyroid function.

NICE NG196: use CHA₂DS₂-VASc. Hers is 3 (age 65–74, female, hypertension). Offer anticoagulation at a score of 2 or more; consider it for men with a score of 1. AF-related strokes tend to be large and disabling.
NICE NG196: assess bleeding risk with ORBIT and address modifiable factors (uncontrolled BP, NSAIDs, alcohol, anaemia). Do not withhold anticoagulation solely because of age or risk of falls.
NICE NG196: do not offer aspirin monotherapy solely for stroke prevention in AF. It gives little protection and still causes bleeding.

NICE NG196 recommends a DOAC (apixaban, dabigatran, edoxaban or rivaroxaban) first-line. No INR monitoring, few food interactions, and lower rates of intracranial bleeding than warfarin in trials. DOACs are not used with mechanical heart valves (BNF), which is why Gordon was on warfarin.
DVLA Group 1: she can drive and need not notify unless AF causes incapacitating symptoms. Review anticoagulation, renal function and bleeding risk at least annually.

dg.d: Let her state her view (“a wobbly tick”) and agreed an agenda that included her choice.
Active, independent, widowed, dog walking and driving; the grandson and neighbour as influences.
Baseline FBC, U&E with creatinine clearance, LFTs, thyroid function; BP check; pulse and symptom review.
Asymptomatic AF with controlled rate; screened for symptoms, bleeding history, falls, NSAIDs and alcohol.
No syncope, chest pain, breathlessness or previous stroke or TIA; stroke risk quantified with CHA₂DS₂-VASc and bleeding with ORBIT.
Explained AF and the clot mechanism in plain words, and why feeling well does not mean low risk.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: DOAC offered per NICE NG196; aspirin explicitly not recommended; decision time with written information and a booked follow-up.
BP optimised; NSAIDs avoided; Gordon’s mechanical-valve warfarin distinguished from her situation.
FAST symptoms mean 999; palpitations, breathlessness or faintness mean a same-day call; next call dated.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Noticed the silence at “blood thinner” and invited Gordon’s story; took the aspirin offer as a cue, not a solution.
Idea (normal ageing, a fussy watch), concern (warfarin killed Gordon), expectation (decline politely, perhaps aspirin).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — Gordon. Warfarin, the ice, the bleed, three days. In her ledger the anticoagulant is the murder weapon, and the doctor on this phone is proposing it for her. She has already decided to refuse; the call is her being polite about it — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Mrs Beech, it’s Dr Lee. Thank you for taking the call. Is now a good time, and are you somewhere you can talk?
model.why: Checks privacy and readiness on the telephone

model.text: Perfectly. And before you start, I feel completely well. The only thing wrong with me is a watch my grandson set up that keeps tutting at me. A wobbly tick at my age, whose isn’t?
I’m very glad you feel well, and that matters. I’d like to explain what the tracing showed, hear what you make of it, and decide together what, if anything, to do. Does that sound all right?
model.why: Clear agenda that includes her view and her choice

model.text: Go ahead.
Have you noticed anything at all: fluttering, breathlessness, dizziness, chest pain or blackouts?
model.why: Screens for symptoms and haemodynamic effect

model.text: Nothing. I walk the dog forty minutes a day, do the garden, drive to the garden centre.
Any bleeding problems, falls, kidney trouble, or do you take ibuprofen or aspirin? And how much alcohol, roughly?
model.why: Bleeding-risk screen before any anticoagulation discussion

model.text: None of that. A sherry at Christmas. Steady as a rock on my feet.

Then here’s what the watch found. The top chambers of your heart aren’t beating in step; they’re quivering. Blood in a small pouch up there moves sluggishly, and still blood can clot. If a clot breaks off, it can travel to the brain and cause a stroke. You can feel perfectly well through all of that, which is why the watch caught it and you didn’t.
model.why: Plain picture of AF and why feeling well and being at risk coexist

model.text: I see. So what do you want to do about it?
The usual treatment is a blood thinner, to stop clots forming.
(Silence.) No. I don’t think so, doctor.
You went quiet when I said blood thinner. Can I ask what that brought up?
model.why: Names the temperature drop and invites the story

model.text: My husband Gordon was on warfarin. For his valve. He slipped on the ice outside the butcher’s, a silly little fall, didn’t even break his glasses. Three days later he was dead. A bleed on the brain. The blood thinner killed him. And now you want to put me on it.

I’m so sorry. Three days, from a fall that didn’t break his glasses. I can understand completely why the tablet is the villain in that story, and on the ice that day it did play its part. Thank you for telling me.
model.why: Receives the grief fully before any pharmacology

model.text: I’ll take an aspirin if it makes you happy. My neighbour Eileen says her cardiologist swears by it.
May I tell you what’s different between Gordon and you? Three things. First, he had a metal valve. For that, warfarin is the only option, even now. The newer tablets can’t be used. He had no choice.
model.why: Honours the story while correcting its categories

model.text: Second, the tablets we use for AF now are different drugs from warfarin. No blood-test clinics, fewer food rules, and in the big trials they caused fewer bleeds into the brain than warfarin. Third, your own bleeding risk is low: no falls, good health, no ibuprofen, and I’ll keep your blood pressure well controlled.
model.why: Distinguishes DOAC from warfarin and personalises bleeding risk

model.text: On aspirin, I have to be honest with you. For this kind of clot it gives very little protection, but it still makes you bleed more easily. National guidance says not to use it for AF. I’d be giving you the risk without the benefit.
model.why: Retires the aspirin compromise kindly and explicitly

model.text: So what are my actual chances, without anything?

We score it from your age, being a woman, and your blood pressure. Your score is three, which puts you in the group where a blood thinner is recommended. Each year without treatment carries a real chance of a stroke, and strokes from AF tend to be the big ones that take speech or movement. Treatment reduces that risk a great deal.
model.why: Makes the CHA₂DS₂-VASc score personal and honest without false precision

model.text: I don’t want to decide on the phone.

You don’t have to. This is your decision. I’ll post you written information, we’ll do some baseline blood tests so the option stays open, and we’ll speak again next week. Your grandson is welcome on that call if you’d like a second pair of ears.
model.why: Hands the decision back with structure, not pressure

model.text: Whatever you decide, one thing holds: if your face droops, an arm goes weak, or your words come out jumbled, that’s 999 straight away. And if you get palpitations, breathlessness or feel faint, ring us the same day.
model.why: FAST safety-net regardless of her decision

model.text: Face, arm, speech, 999. I know that one from the adverts.
Exactly. I’ll book the call for Tuesday. And keep the watch on; it did you a favour.
model.why: Dated follow-up and a positive reframe of the watch

model.text: (Small laugh.) I’ll tell him you said so. Tuesday, then.

social.t: A spouse’s death on an anticoagulant makes the drug the villain of the family story. Grief must be heard before information can land.
She values her dog, garden and driving. Stroke is the real threat to that independence, which is a useful frame if she chooses it.

legal.t: Group 1: AF does not need to be reported unless it causes symptoms that may distract or incapacitate the driver (DVLA Assessing fitness to drive).
She has capacity and may decline. An informed refusal is recorded as today’s decision, with the offer repeated at review.

professional.t: Present benefits and risks in terms she understands, respect her choice and record the discussion (GMC Decision making and consent 2020).
Do not oversell DOAC safety or understate stroke risk; balanced information is part of valid consent.

community.t: Arrhythmia Alliance and Stroke Association information; bereavement support if Gordon’s death is still raw; community pharmacy New Medicine Service if a DOAC is started.

redFlags: Syncope, chest pain or breathlessness with AF: same-day assessment
Face drooping, arm weakness or speech disturbance: 999
Bleeding history, anaemia, NSAID use or uncontrolled BP: address before or alongside anticoagulation
psychosocial: Widowed; husband died of an intracranial bleed on warfarin after a fall
Independent, active, drives, lives with her dog
Grandson and neighbour influencing her views
ice: Idea: “A wobbly tick at my age, a fussy watch.”
Concern: the blood thinner that she believes killed Gordon
Expectation: decline politely, perhaps take aspirin

playbook.diagnosis: New asymptomatic atrial fibrillation, rate 88, confirmed on 12-lead ECG. CHA₂DS₂-VASc 3 (age 65–74, female, hypertension): anticoagulation indicated per NICE NG196. Bleeding risk appears low.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “The top chambers of your heart are quivering rather than beating. That doesn’t make you feel ill, but blood can pool and clot there, and a clot can travel to the brain and cause a stroke. The treatment is about preventing that.”

management.reflectIce: “The blood thinner is tied up with losing Gordon, and I’m not going to argue with your grief. Can I show you what’s different about his situation and yours?”
management.psychosocial: Give time and written information; invite the grandson to the next call; offer bereavement support if wanted.
sharedPlan: Offer a DOAC per NICE NG196; explain the difference from warfarin and why aspirin is not recommended
Baseline FBC, U&E with creatinine clearance, LFTs, thyroid function; BP optimised; avoid NSAIDs
Follow-up call booked for next week; decision hers
safetyNet: Palpitations, breathlessness or faintness: same-day call; annual AF review

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed by talking pharmacology through a silence. Gordon arrives before his name does; hear him first, then separate his story from hers.

items.fail: Accepting aspirin as a reasonable compromise.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” NICE NG196 advises against aspirin monotherapy for AF stroke prevention.
items.fix: Say it plainly and kindly: little protection, real bleeding risk, not recommended.

items.fail: Reassuring her that asymptomatic AF needs nothing because she feels well.
items.why: Symptoms do not predict stroke risk; CHA₂DS₂-VASc does, and hers is 3.
items.fix: Explain the still-blood mechanism and why the watch caught what she could not feel.

items.why: NICE NG196 asks for bleeding assessment (ORBIT) and management of modifiable risks; it is also what reassures a frightened patient.
items.fix: Ask about falls, bleeding, NSAIDs and alcohol, and say out loud what you will optimise.

items.fail: Carrying on with DOAC facts after she goes quiet.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to the patient’s cues.” The silence is Gordon.
items.fix: “You went quiet when I said blood thinner. What did that bring up?”

items.fail: Pressing for a decision on the call.
items.why: Pressure turns hesitation into a lasting refusal and fails the shared-decision marks.
items.fix: Written information, the grandson invited, a dated follow-up call, and a record that the door stays open.

items.fail: No safety-net because she has declined treatment.
items.why: Non-specific or absent safety-netting is a standard failing statement, and her stroke risk is unchanged by her decision.
items.fix: FAST means 999 whatever she decides; palpitations or breathlessness mean a same-day call.

timeMap.d: She opens with “I feel perfectly well”. Accept it, then agree to explain the result and decide together.
Palpitations, breathlessness, dizziness, chest pain; falls, bleeding, NSAIDs, alcohol.
Quivering chambers, still blood, clots. When she goes quiet at “blood thinner”, ask. Hear Gordon in full.
Metal valve versus AF; DOAC versus warfarin; her low bleeding risk; aspirin retired kindly; CHA₂DS₂-VASc 3.
Written information, baseline bloods, grandson invited, call booked. FAST 999 whatever she decides.

wordPics.fail: Prescribes a DOAC over her objection or accepts aspirin as a compromise; talks pharmacology through the silence and never hears about Gordon; no stroke-risk explanation; no FAST safety-net.
wordPics.pass: Explains AF and stroke risk, recommends a DOAC, says aspirin is not appropriate, listens to her concern about Gordon, offers time and follow-up with basic safety-netting.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: stops at the silence and hears Gordon before any drug facts; separates the metal valve and warfarin from her situation point by point; screens and optimises bleeding risk out loud; hands the decision back with written information, the grandson invited and a dated call.

avoid.dont: “Aspirin is better than nothing, so let’s start that for now.”
avoid.instead: “For this kind of clot aspirin gives very little protection but still makes you bleed more. I’d be giving you the risk without the benefit.”
avoid.why: NICE NG196 advises against aspirin monotherapy for stroke prevention in AF.

avoid.dont: “The new tablets are completely safe, nothing like warfarin.”
avoid.instead: “They do carry some bleeding risk, but less bleeding into the brain than warfarin, and yours is low.”
avoid.why: Overselling destroys trust with someone who has lived through a fatal bleed.

avoid.dont: “You really need to start this today.”
avoid.instead: “This is your decision. Take the week, read the information, and we’ll talk on Tuesday.”
avoid.why: Pressure produces a firm no; structured time produces a considered choice.

You don’t have to. This is your decision. I’ll post you written information, we’ll do some baseline blood tests so the option stays open, and we’ll speak again next week. Your grandson is welcome on that call if you’d like a second pair of ears.
SCA_MODELS.why: Hands the decision back with structure, not pressure

SCA_MODELS.text: Whatever you decide, one thing holds: if your face droops, an arm goes weak, or your words come out jumbled, that’s 999 straight away. And if you get palpitations, breathlessness or feel faint, ring us the same day.
SCA_MODELS.why: FAST safety-net regardless of her decision

SCA_MODELS.text: Face, arm, speech, 999. I know that one from the adverts.
Exactly. I’ll book the call for Tuesday. And keep the watch on; it did you a favour.
SCA_MODELS.why: Dated follow-up and a positive reframe of the watch

SCA_MODELS.text: (Small laugh.) I’ll tell him you said so. Tuesday, then.

SCA_STEM.name: Sylvia Beech
SCA_STEM.recent: Smartwatch alerts for irregular rhythm. Practice 12-lead ECG last week: atrial fibrillation, rate 88. BP 138/82. No diabetes, no previous stroke or TIA. Widowed 2021 (husband Gordon, on warfarin for a metallic valve, died of an intracranial bleed after a fall).
SCA_STEM.reason: Telephone call to discuss the ECG result.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG196 (atrial fibrillation) · BNF (direct-acting oral anticoagulants) · DVLA Assessing fitness to drive
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Asymptomatic AF found by a wearable and confirmed on ECG is a stroke-prevention decision. Her CHA₂DS₂-VASc is 3, so anticoagulation with a DOAC should be offered; aspirin is not an alternative.

points.t: A wearable alert needs ECG confirmation, which she has. Rate 88 at rest with no symptoms means rate control is not the pressing issue; stroke risk is. Baseline FBC, U&E with creatinine clearance, LFTs and thyroid function.

NICE NG196: use CHA₂DS₂-VASc. Hers is 3 (age 65–74, female, hypertension). Offer anticoagulation at a score of 2 or more; consider it for men with a score of 1. AF-related strokes tend to be large and disabling.
NICE NG196: assess bleeding risk with ORBIT and address modifiable factors (uncontrolled BP, NSAIDs, alcohol, anaemia). Do not withhold anticoagulation solely because of age or risk of falls.
NICE NG196: do not offer aspirin monotherapy solely for stroke prevention in AF. It gives little protection and still causes bleeding.

NICE NG196 recommends a DOAC (apixaban, dabigatran, edoxaban or rivaroxaban) first-line. No INR monitoring, few food interactions, and lower rates of intracranial bleeding than warfarin in trials. DOACs are not used with mechanical heart valves (BNF), which is why Gordon was on warfarin.
DVLA Group 1: she can drive and need not notify unless AF causes incapacitating symptoms. Review anticoagulation, renal function and bleeding risk at least annually.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Let her state her view (“a wobbly tick”) and agreed an agenda that included her choice.
Active, independent, widowed, dog walking and driving; the grandson and neighbour as influences.
Noticed the silence at “blood thinner” and invited Gordon’s story; took the aspirin offer as a cue, not a solution.
Idea (normal ageing, a fussy watch), concern (warfarin killed Gordon), expectation (decline politely, perhaps aspirin).
Baseline FBC, U&E with creatinine clearance, LFTs, thyroid function; BP check; pulse and symptom review.
Asymptomatic AF with controlled rate; screened for symptoms, bleeding history, falls, NSAIDs and alcohol.
No syncope, chest pain, breathlessness or previous stroke or TIA; stroke risk quantified with CHA₂DS₂-VASc and bleeding with ORBIT.
Explained AF and the clot mechanism in plain words, and why feeling well does not mean low risk.
DOAC offered per NICE NG196; aspirin explicitly not recommended; decision time with written information and a booked follow-up.
BP optimised; NSAIDs avoided; Gordon’s mechanical-valve warfarin distinguished from her situation.
FAST symptoms mean 999; palpitations, breathlessness or faintness mean a same-day call; next call dated.

social.t: A spouse’s death on an anticoagulant makes the drug the villain of the family story. Grief must be heard before information can land.
She values her dog, garden and driving. Stroke is the real threat to that independence, which is a useful frame if she chooses it.

legal.t: Group 1: AF does not need to be reported unless it causes symptoms that may distract or incapacitate the driver (DVLA Assessing fitness to drive).
She has capacity and may decline. An informed refusal is recorded as today’s decision, with the offer repeated at review.

professional.t: Present benefits and risks in terms she understands, respect her choice and record the discussion (GMC Decision making and consent 2020).
Do not oversell DOAC safety or understate stroke risk; balanced information is part of valid consent.

community.t: Arrhythmia Alliance and Stroke Association information; bereavement support if Gordon’s death is still raw; community pharmacy New Medicine Service if a DOAC is started.

redFlags: Syncope, chest pain or breathlessness with AF: same-day assessment
Face drooping, arm weakness or speech disturbance: 999
Bleeding history, anaemia, NSAID use or uncontrolled BP: address before or alongside anticoagulation
psychosocial: Widowed; husband died of an intracranial bleed on warfarin after a fall
Independent, active, drives, lives with her dog
Grandson and neighbour influencing her views
ice: Idea: “A wobbly tick at my age, a fussy watch.”
Concern: the blood thinner that she believes killed Gordon
Expectation: decline politely, perhaps take aspirin

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: New asymptomatic atrial fibrillation, rate 88, confirmed on 12-lead ECG. CHA₂DS₂-VASc 3 (age 65–74, female, hypertension): anticoagulation indicated per NICE NG196. Bleeding risk appears low.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “The top chambers of your heart are quivering rather than beating. That doesn’t make you feel ill, but blood can pool and clot there, and a clot can travel to the brain and cause a stroke. The treatment is about preventing that.”

management.reflectIce: “The blood thinner is tied up with losing Gordon, and I’m not going to argue with your grief. Can I show you what’s different about his situation and yours?”
management.psychosocial: Give time and written information; invite the grandson to the next call; offer bereavement support if wanted.
sharedPlan: Offer a DOAC per NICE NG196; explain the difference from warfarin and why aspirin is not recommended
Baseline FBC, U&E with creatinine clearance, LFTs, thyroid function; BP optimised; avoid NSAIDs
Follow-up call booked for next week; decision hers
safetyNet: Palpitations, breathlessness or faintness: same-day call; annual AF review

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed by talking pharmacology through a silence. Gordon arrives before his name does; hear him first, then separate his story from hers.

items.fail: Accepting aspirin as a reasonable compromise.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” NICE NG196 advises against aspirin monotherapy for AF stroke prevention.
items.fix: Say it plainly and kindly: little protection, real bleeding risk, not recommended.

items.fail: Reassuring her that asymptomatic AF needs nothing because she feels well.
items.why: Symptoms do not predict stroke risk; CHA₂DS₂-VASc does, and hers is 3.
items.fix: Explain the still-blood mechanism and why the watch caught what she could not feel.

items.why: NICE NG196 asks for bleeding assessment (ORBIT) and management of modifiable risks; it is also what reassures a frightened patient.
items.fix: Ask about falls, bleeding, NSAIDs and alcohol, and say out loud what you will optimise.

items.fail: Carrying on with DOAC facts after she goes quiet.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to the patient’s cues.” The silence is Gordon.
items.fix: “You went quiet when I said blood thinner. What did that bring up?”

items.fail: Pressing for a decision on the call.
items.why: Pressure turns hesitation into a lasting refusal and fails the shared-decision marks.
items.fix: Written information, the grandson invited, a dated follow-up call, and a record that the door stays open.

items.fail: No safety-net because she has declined treatment.
items.why: Non-specific or absent safety-netting is a standard failing statement, and her stroke risk is unchanged by her decision.
items.fix: FAST means 999 whatever she decides; palpitations or breathlessness mean a same-day call.
